title: Illinois County Public Health Analysis
text:
This project examines community health needs, healthcare access, and geographic differences across Illinois. By integrating hospital Community Health Needs Assessments (CHNAs), local health department Illinois Project for Local Assessment of Needs (IPLAN) priorities, and county-level demographic and socioeconomic data, the analysis explores how public health priorities and community characteristics vary across the state.
A central focus of the project is examining alignment between hospital-identified health needs and local public health priorities. Analyses also explore how geographic location, poverty, insurance coverage, and population characteristics relate to differences in community health priorities. Together, these findings provide insight into the distribution of health needs and disparities across Illinois.

title: Illinois County Public Health Analysis
text:
Project Objectives

Compare community health priorities: Examine alignment and differences between hospital CHNA and local health department IPLAN priorities.
Explore geographic variation: Identify differences in health priorities across Chicago, Suburban Cook, Suburban Non-Cook, Urban Non-Cook, and Rural areas.
Examine socioeconomic patterns: Explore how poverty and uninsured rates relate to the health priorities identified by local jurisdictions.
Assess population characteristics: Examine demographic and socioeconomic differences across Illinois counties.
Inform public health planning: Present findings through data visualizations and geographic comparisons to support discussions about community health needs, healthcare access, and resource allocation.

title: Illinois County Public Health Analysis
text:
Project Report and Documentation
The accompanying report provides a detailed overview of the project background, data sources, methodology, analytical approach, and findings. It includes descriptive statistics, comparisons of hospital and public health priorities, geographic analyses, and socioeconomic comparisons.

title: Illinois County Public Health Analysis
text:
Intended Audience
The intended audience includes Illinois public health professionals, policymakers, healthcare organizations, local health departments, and community stakeholders. This project also supports ongoing work with the Illinois Department of Public Health (IDPH) to develop a statewide Report on Patient Access to Care for the Illinois General Assembly. The analysis is intended to help inform policymakers about healthcare access, population health needs, and geographic inequities across Illinois.

title: Illinois County Public Health Analysis
text:
Major Findings
The analysis highlights differences and areas of alignment between hospital Community Health Needs Assessments (CHNAs) and county-level Illinois Project for Local Assessment of Needs (IPLANs). Comparing these priorities provides insight into how healthcare organizations and local public health departments identify and address community health needs.
Geographic and socioeconomic characteristics, including poverty, insurance coverage, population demographics, and rurality, provide additional context for understanding differences in community health priorities across Illinois. The findings emphasize the importance of examining health needs within their local geographic and socioeconomic contexts.

title: Illinois County Public Health Analysis
text:
Recommendations
Based on the analysis, the following recommendations can help strengthen community health planning and resource allocation across Illinois:

Strengthen collaboration: Encourage greater coordination between hospitals and local health departments to align community health priorities and develop shared strategies.
Address health inequities: Prioritize communities experiencing greater socioeconomic disadvantages and barriers to healthcare access.
Use geographic data for planning: Incorporate GIS mapping and county-level demographic information to identify underserved areas and guide resource allocation.
Improve data consistency: Promote standardized reporting, consistent priority classifications, and more complete community health assessment data to support meaningful comparisons across counties and healthcare organizations.

title: Illinois County Public Health Analysis
text:
Lessons Learned
This project demonstrated the importance of integrating multiple data sources to better understand community health needs and geographic differences across Illinois.
Several lessons emerged throughout the analysis:

Data quality and availability matter: Differences in reporting periods, assessment methods, and data completeness can affect comparisons between hospitals and counties.
Geographic context is essential: Statewide patterns may overlook important differences between urban, suburban, and rural communities.
Standardization improves comparisons: Consistent categorization of health priorities makes it easier to identify areas of overlap and differences across assessments.
Multiple data sources provide a broader perspective: Combining hospital assessments, county health priorities, and demographic and socioeconomic indicators provides a more comprehensive understanding of community health needs.

Overall, this analysis reinforces the value of data-driven public health planning that considers both identified health priorities and the geographic and socioeconomic conditions that shape community health.

title: Methodology
text:
This analysis integrates hospital Community Health Needs Assessments (CHNAs), local health department Illinois Project for Local Assessment of Needs (IPLAN) assessments, and county-level demographic and socioeconomic data.
Hospital CHNA reports and local health department IPLAN assessments were used to identify and compare community health priorities across Illinois. Demographic and socioeconomic indicators, including population, age distribution, racial and ethnic composition, poverty, median household income, and health insurance coverage, were obtained from the U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey (ACS) 5-Year Estimates.
County rurality classifications were obtained from the USDA Economic Research Service (ERS) Rural-Urban Continuum Codes (RUCC). These data were incorporated to examine geographic differences across Illinois.

text:
This analysis integrates hospital Community Health Needs Assessments (CHNAs), local health department Illinois Project for Local Assessment of Needs (IPLAN) assessments, and county-level demographic and socioeconomic data.
Hospital CHNA reports and local health department IPLAN assessments were used to identify and compare community health priorities across Illinois. title: Methodology
text:
Data Preparation
Hospital CHNA and local health department IPLAN datasets were organized separately and standardized into consistent health topic categories to facilitate comparisons across assessment sources.
Geographic classifications were established to distinguish five mutually exclusive groups: Chicago, Suburban Cook, Suburban Non-Cook, Urban Non-Cook, and Rural. Chicago was analyzed separately from the remainder of Cook County to distinguish municipal and suburban health priorities.
Demographic and socioeconomic indicators were integrated into the county-level dataset using geographic identifiers. Population, poverty, income, insurance coverage, age, and racial and ethnic composition variables were prepared for descriptive and comparative analyses.
Counties were also stratified into higher- and lower-poverty groups and higher- and lower-uninsured groups to examine differences in first-ranked IPLAN priorities across socioeconomic conditions.

title: Methodology
text:
Analytical Methods
Descriptive Statistics: Means, standard deviations, medians, minimums, and maximums were calculated to summarize county-level demographic, socioeconomic, and healthcare access characteristics. Sample sizes and missing observations were also examined.
Priority Comparisons: Hospital CHNA and local health department IPLAN priorities were summarized by health topic and geographic group. Frequency distributions were used to identify commonly reported priorities and differences between assessment sources.
Priority Alignment and Overlap: Shared CHNA and IPLAN priorities were compared across geographic groups. Overlap was calculated as the number of shared health priorities divided by the total number of unique priorities identified by both assessment sources, multiplied by 100.
First-Ranked Priority Analysis: The highest-ranked CHNA and IPLAN priorities were examined separately across the five geographic groups. Frequencies were calculated to identify differences in the primary health needs emphasized by hospitals and local health departments.
Geographic Distribution of Priorities: The geographic distribution of hospital CHNA and county IPLAN priorities was examined across standardized health topic categories. Percentages were calculated to identify the contribution of each geographic group to the total assessments identifying a particular priority.
Priority Prevalence: The prevalence of three selected health priorities was examined across geographic groups. For hospital CHNAs, Behavioral and Mental Health, Access to Care and Healthcare Equity, and Chronic Disease Management were compared. For IPLAN assessments, Behavioral and Mental Health, Chronic Disease Management, and Healthy Behaviors and Wellness were examined. Percentages were calculated using the number of assessments within each geographic group.
Cook County and Chicago Comparison: Hospital CHNA priorities were compared with the corresponding local health department IPLAN priorities in Chicago and Suburban Cook. The Chicago Department of Public Health and Cook County Department of Public Health assessments were examined separately to identify similarities and differences in institutional priorities.
Ordered IPLAN Priority Comparison: The five ranked health priorities selected by the Chicago Department of Public Health and Cook County Department of Public Health were compared in their original order to examine differences in priority selection.
Socioeconomic Stratification: First-ranked IPLAN priorities were examined across higher- and lower-poverty and higher- and lower-uninsured county groups. Percentages were calculated to explore differences in the distribution of leading public health priorities across socioeconomic classifications.

title: Methodology
text:
Data Visualization
Data visualizations were developed using R and ggplot2 to examine health priority distributions, geographic differences, priority alignment, and socioeconomic patterns. Statistical summaries and comparative graphs were used to present differences between hospital and local health department assessments.
Geographic data were incorporated into an interactive GIS dashboard to display county-level demographic, socioeconomic, and healthcare access indicators across Illinois. The dashboard allows users to explore individual data layers and examine geographic patterns in population characteristics and resource availability.

title: Health Priorities & Population
text:
This section presents a collection of data visualizations examining hospital Community Health Needs Assessments (CHNAs), local health department Illinois Project for Local Assessment of Needs (IPLAN) priorities, and demographic and socioeconomic characteristics across Illinois. Analyses are organized across five geographic groups: Chicago, Suburban Cook, Suburban Non-Cook, Urban Non-Cook, and Rural.
Using hospital assessment data, local health department priorities, U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey (ACS) estimates, and geographic classifications, these analyses examine alignment between healthcare institutions and local public health departments. Interactive graphs, statistical comparisons, and geographic visualizations highlight differences in community health priorities, population characteristics, and socioeconomic conditions to inform public health planning and policy decisions.



Methods: Descriptive statistics were calculated for county-level demographic, socioeconomic, and healthcare access indicators. Measures included sample size, mean, standard deviation, median, minimum, and maximum.
Interpretation: The average county poverty rate was approximately 12%, with a median of 13%. Mean median household income was approximately $79,491. County population showed substantial variation, with the mean considerably higher than the median, reflecting the influence of highly populated areas.




Methods: Hospital CHNA and local health department IPLAN priorities were standardized into common health topic categories and compared across five geographic groups. Shared priorities were identified within each group. Alignment was calculated as the number of shared priorities divided by the total number of unique priorities, multiplied by 100.
Interpretation: Overall, CHNA and IPLAN assessments shared 9 of 10 unique health priorities statewide, representing 90% overlap. Suburban Non-Cook demonstrated the highest alignment (77.8%), followed by Rural (62.5%) and Chicago (55.6%). Suburban Cook (37.5%) and Urban Non-Cook (33.3%) demonstrated the lowest alignment. Although statewide alignment was high, differences across geographic groups suggest that hospitals and local health departments do not always identify the same community health needs.





Methods: Hospital CHNA first-ranked priorities were examined across the five geographic groups. The number of hospitals identifying each health topic as their highest-ranked priority was calculated and compared by geographic location.
Interpretation: Behavioral and Mental Health was the leading first-ranked hospital priority in Chicago (12 hospitals), Suburban Cook (10), and Urban Non-Cook (31). Rural hospitals were divided between Behavioral and Mental Health and Access to Care and Healthcare Equity (6 each). Suburban Non-Cook hospitals identified Access to Care and Healthcare Equity as their leading first-ranked priority (11 hospitals). These findings demonstrate geographic variation in the primary health needs emphasized by hospitals.





Methods: First-ranked IPLAN priorities were examined across the five geographic groups. The frequency of each leading health topic was calculated to identify differences in the primary priorities selected by local health departments.
Interpretation: Behavioral and Mental Health was the leading first-ranked priority in Urban Non-Cook (10 assessments), Suburban Non-Cook (7), and Rural jurisdictions (7). In contrast, Chicago and Suburban Cook identified Chronic Disease Management as their first-ranked priority. These findings demonstrate differences between hospital and public health department priorities across geographic areas.




Methods: Hospital CHNA priorities were grouped by geographic location and standardized across ten health topic categories. The proportion of hospital assessments identifying each priority was calculated within each topic to examine its geographic distribution.
Interpretation: The geographic distribution of hospital priorities varied by health topic. Behavioral and Mental Health and Chronic Disease Management were represented across multiple geographic groups. Substance Abuse was exclusively represented in rural hospital assessments. Other topics, including Maternal, Infant, and Child Health and Injury Prevention and Safety, also demonstrated differences in geographic representation.




Methods: County and Chicago IPLAN priorities were grouped into the five geographic classifications. The proportion of IPLAN assessments identifying each health topic was calculated to examine the geographic distribution of reported priorities.
Interpretation: Substance Abuse was exclusively represented in rural IPLAN assessments. Urban and suburban jurisdictions contributed substantially to priorities such as Infectious Disease Prevention and Control, Injury Prevention and Safety, and Social Determinants of Health. These findings illustrate how local public health priorities vary across geographic settings.




Methods: Three frequently identified hospital CHNA priorities were selected for comparison: Behavioral and Mental Health, Access to Care and Healthcare Equity, and Chronic Disease Management. The percentage of hospitals identifying each priority was calculated within each geographic group.
Interpretation: Behavioral and Mental Health demonstrated consistently high prevalence across all geographic groups, ranging from 73.9% in Suburban Non-Cook to 96.6% in Chicago. Chronic Disease Management showed considerable geographic variation, with the highest prevalence in Suburban Cook (85.0%) and the lowest in Rural areas (31.2%). Access to Care and Healthcare Equity was also commonly identified, although its prevalence varied across regions.




Methods: Three frequently identified IPLAN priorities were examined across geographic groups: Behavioral and Mental Health, Chronic Disease Management, and Healthy Behaviors and Wellness. The percentage of local health department assessments identifying each priority was calculated within each group.
Interpretation: Behavioral and Mental Health and Chronic Disease Management were identified in 100% of both Chicago and Suburban Cook IPLAN assessments. Behavioral and Mental Health was also prevalent in Rural (100%), Suburban Non-Cook (88.2%), and Urban Non-Cook (89.7%) jurisdictions. Healthy Behaviors and Wellness was most frequently identified in Rural jurisdictions (57.1%), followed by Suburban Non-Cook (41.2%).
Data consideration: Chicago and Suburban Cook each have one IPLAN observation, so their percentages represent individual assessments rather than broader jurisdictional patterns.




Methods: Hospital CHNA priorities were compared with local health department IPLAN priorities in Chicago and Suburban Cook. Chicago hospital assessments were compared with the Chicago Department of Public Health (CDPH) IPLAN, while Cook County hospital assessments outside Chicago were compared with the Cook County Department of Public Health (CCDPH) IPLAN. The percentage of assessments identifying each health topic was calculated to examine institutional differences.
Interpretation: Hospital and public health department assessments demonstrated alignment in Behavioral and Mental Health and Chronic Disease Management. However, hospitals placed additional emphasis on Access to Care and Healthcare Equity and Social Determinants of Health. Access to Care reached approximately 75% among hospital assessments, while Social Determinants of Health reached approximately 55.2%. These priorities were not represented in the municipal IPLAN frameworks, highlighting differences in the health needs emphasized by clinical institutions and local public health departments.




Methods: The five ranked IPLAN priorities selected by the Chicago Department of Public Health and Cook County Department of Public Health were compared in their original order of selection. Each priority was organized by rank to identify similarities and differences in the jurisdictions’ stated priorities.
Interpretation: Both Chicago and Suburban Cook identified Chronic Disease Management as their first-ranked priority. However, their subsequent rankings differed. Chicago placed greater emphasis on Injury Prevention and Safety and Infectious Disease Prevention and Control, while Suburban Cook prioritized Maternal, Infant, and Child Health and Behavioral and Mental Health in its second and third positions. These differences illustrate how neighboring jurisdictions can identify different areas of public health emphasis.




Methods: Counties were stratified into higher- and lower-poverty groups and higher- and lower-uninsured groups. The distribution of first-ranked IPLAN priorities was compared across these socioeconomic classifications. The percentage of counties within each group identifying each priority was calculated.
Interpretation: Behavioral and Mental Health remained the leading first-ranked priority across poverty and uninsured classifications, representing approximately 53–57% of counties.

Poverty: Higher-poverty counties identified Chronic Disease Management more frequently than lower-poverty counties (35% versus 13%). Conversely, Access to Care and Healthcare Equity was more common among lower-poverty counties (30.4% versus 10%).
Uninsured status: Behavioral and Mental Health remained the leading priority across both uninsured groups (53.3–57.1%). Chronic Disease Management represented 26.7% of higher-uninsured counties compared with 21.4% of lower-uninsured counties.

These findings suggest that socioeconomic characteristics may be associated with differences in the health priorities selected by local public health departments.



The interactive GIS dashboard provides a geographic view of county-level demographic, socioeconomic, and healthcare access indicators across Illinois.
Methods: County-level data were integrated with geographic boundary files to create interactive maps. Variables include population characteristics, poverty, insurance coverage, age distribution, racial and ethnic composition, and geographic classifications. Map layers allow users to examine individual indicators and compare their distributions across counties.
Interpretation: Geographic visualization provides additional context for understanding the distribution of demographic and socioeconomic characteristics across Illinois. Differences in population composition, poverty, and insurance coverage can help identify geographic areas where additional public health attention or healthcare resources may be needed.



Findings reflect available hospital CHNA reports, local health department IPLAN assessments, and county-level demographic and socioeconomic data. Not all counties and hospitals had available assessment information, and reporting years varied. Geographic comparisons were organized into five mutually defined groups to distinguish Chicago from Suburban Cook and other urban and rural areas.
Some geographic comparisons, particularly Chicago and Suburban Cook IPLAN analyses, are based on a single local health department assessment. These findings should therefore be interpreted as jurisdiction-specific observations rather than estimates representative of multiple jurisdictions.
Demographic and socioeconomic comparisons are based on aggregated county-level data and should not be interpreted as evidence of individual-level relationships or causation. Additionally, the frequency with which a health topic is identified reflects assessment priorities and does not necessarily measure the prevalence or severity of the underlying health condition.

title: GIS Map
text:
This interactive geographic information system (GIS) map explores county-level differences in population demographics, socioeconomic conditions, healthcare access, and community health priorities throughout Illinois.
The map allows users to examine how health-related indicators vary across counties and geographic groups. Select different map layers to explore demographic characteristics, healthcare access, and hospital and community health priorities.
How to use the map:

Select an indicator using the layer controls.
Hover over a county to view its name, population, and indicator value.
Compare county-level patterns across Illinois.
Use the geographic group boundaries to identify broader regional patterns.

title: GIS Map
text:
Geographic Group Comparison
Illinois counties are organized into geographic groups to examine differences in population characteristics, socioeconomic conditions, and healthcare access.
The map displays county boundaries alongside geographic group boundaries to distinguish individual county patterns from broader regional patterns.

Geographic Groups

Urban: Counties classified as urban.
Suburban: Counties classified as suburban.
Rural: Counties classified as rural.

Use the map to explore how demographic and healthcare indicators vary across these geographic groups.

title: GIS Map
text:
Geographic Patterns and Interpretation
The geographic distribution of health indicators can help identify areas where population characteristics, socioeconomic conditions, and healthcare resources differ.
Consider the following when interpreting the map:

Population demographics: How do age and racial and ethnic compositions vary across counties?
Socioeconomic conditions: Where are poverty rates higher?
Healthcare access: How does the uninsured population vary geographically? Where are hospital resources concentrated?
Community health priorities: Do CHNA and IPLAN priorities appear consistent across counties and geographic groups?

These patterns provide geographic context for the findings presented in the Health Priorities and Population & Healthcare Access sections of this dashboard.

title: GIS Map
text:
Data Notes and Limitations

Geographic unit: Illinois counties.
Geographic classification: Urban, Suburban, and Rural.
Population: County-level population estimates.
Demographic indicators: Age and racial and ethnic composition.
Socioeconomic indicators: Poverty and health insurance coverage.
Healthcare indicators: Number of hospitals in each county.
Community health priorities: Top three priorities identified in hospital CHNAs and county IPLANs.

County-level data represent aggregated population characteristics and should not be interpreted as individual-level outcomes.
Differences in data availability, reporting periods, and source methodologies may affect comparisons across counties.
